summary: The submitted solution does not solve the stated Two Sum problem: it searches for elements equal to target rather than finding a pair that sums to target. As a result, it passed only the single visible test that likely matched that misinterpretation, and failed all other basic/edge cases.

test_results.summary_note: Passed 1/10; failed all meaningful Two Sum scenarios (pairs, duplicates, negatives, two-element case) because the implementation checks nums[i] == target rather than nums[i] + nums[j] == target.

dimensions.name: Correctness & Completeness
dimensions.label: needs work
dimensions.what_went_well: The function runs without errors and returns indices in a deterministic format (a list).
dimensions.what_to_improve: Core requirement was missed: find two indices whose values sum to target. This led to failures on "basic pair" (expected [0,1] got []), "pair at end", "duplicates", "negative numbers", and "two elements".

dimensions.name: Problem-Solving & Thinking
dimensions.label: needs work
dimensions.what_went_well: You produced a working loop-based scan and a concrete output structure under time pressure.
dimensions.what_to_improve: The main issue was problem comprehension/translation to logic. Two Sum requires reasoning about complements (target - x) and tracking prior elements, plus ensuring you don’t use the same element twice.

dimensions.name: Technical Communication
dimensions.label: needs work
dimensions.what_went_well: You responded to prompts and indicated progress status ("Still working", "mostly done").
dimensions.what_to_improve: You didn’t articulate an approach or validate understanding when asked to walk through it. In interviews, stating the plan (hash map of seen values to index; for each x check target-x) helps catch misreads early.

dimensions.name: Complexity & Optimization
dimensions.label: needs work
dimensions.what_went_well: Current code is O(n) time and O(1) extra space (excluding output list), which is efficient as a scan.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Even though it’s O(n), it’s optimizing the wrong computation. The expected canonical approach is also O(n) but uses a hash map to actually find a valid pair; your implementation doesn’t address the required operation.

dimensions.name: Code Quality
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: Simple, readable structure; no unnecessary complexity; clear variable names for a short snippet.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Return shape should match the problem: exactly two indices. Also, avoid building a list of all matches unless the spec asks for it (here, exactly one valid answer exists).

dimensions.name: Independence
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: No hints were used and you produced a complete submission on your own.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Independence is less valuable if you’re independently going down the wrong path; practice the habit of restating the problem in your own words and checking with the interviewer before coding.

thinking_and_logic: Based on the final code and failures, the implemented logic was: scan for indices where nums[i] equals target. Two Sum instead requires identifying two distinct indices (i, j) such that nums[i] + nums[j] == target. A standard way is to iterate once while keeping a dictionary from value to index; for each value x at index i, compute need = target - x, and if need has been seen, return [seen_index, i]. This also naturally prevents using the same element twice (because you only match with previously seen indices).
code_assessment: The code is syntactically correct and clean, but it implements a different problem (finding elements equal to target). That mismatch explains the test outcomes: it returns [] for cases where no element equals target even though a valid pair exists, including duplicates and negative-number scenarios. It also returns a variable-length list, whereas the problem expects exactly two indices for the single valid pair.

next_steps.action: Adopt a 20-second 'restate + example' routine before coding
next_steps.why: This would likely have caught the misread immediately (target as a sum vs target as a value match).
next_steps.how: Say: 'We need indices i,j where nums[i]+nums[j]=target; e.g., [2,7,11,15], target=9 => [0,1]. Exactly one answer, cannot reuse same element.' Then confirm and start coding.

next_steps.action: Practice the canonical One-Pass Hash Map pattern for Two Sum and variants
next_steps.why: It’s the expected optimal solution (O(n) time) and generalizes to many interview problems.
next_steps.how: Implement from memory: dict value->index; loop i,x; if target-x in dict return [dict[target-x], i]; else dict[x]=i. Drill on duplicates (e.g., [3,3], target=6) and negatives.

next_steps.action: Add a quick self-test checklist before submitting
next_steps.why: A couple of manual tests would have revealed the logic gap even without hints.
next_steps.how: Before submit, run mentally: (1) smallest case [a,b]; (2) duplicates; (3) negatives; (4) 'pair at end'. Ensure output is exactly two indices.

patterns_to_study: handling duplicates without using the same index twice
encouragement: This is a very fixable miss: once you lock in the habit of restating the requirement and running 2–3 mental examples, Two Sum becomes a straightforward hash-map exercise you can reliably complete under time.
